input.rationale: Trace how a restarted node re-establishes its configuration ('context validity') when the committed-log replay feature is enabled. NewRaft replays committed logs first (restoreFromCommittedLogs sets lastApplied to the persisted commit index) and then scans the log for configuration entries starting at max(lastSnapshot, lastApplied)+1. Because the scan is skipped over the committed prefix, configuration entries inside it are never applied to r.configurations when no snapshot carries them, even though they remain in the log. Focused probe: restart a single-voter node that was bootstrapped and applied commands but never snapshotted, with RestoreCommittedLogs on/off and with a covering snapshot as control. Reproducibility question: the dual-majority outcome depends on the ordering between the partitioned side's election and the stale leader's lease, so its successor experiment is repeated once from its retained inputs in a clean copy to see whether the concurrent-leader window and the truncation of the committed entry recur under schedule variation. Reproducibility question: the corrected resurrected-voter experiment is repeated once from its retained inputs in a clean copy, because the premature-commit observation depends on the stale leader winning its re-election after the restart and on the removed voter having caught up before the partition. Reproducibility question: the forgotten-added-voter experiment is repeated once from its retained inputs in a clean copy, since the premature commit depends on the restarted leader winning its re-election with an understated quorum and on the partition leaving exactly two connected voters. Reproducibility question: the three-voter simultaneous-restart experiment is repeated once from its retained inputs in a clean copy, because the progress claim (no leader while every voter holds the configuration only in its log) is the headline liveness consequence and currently rests on a single scored execution with its control. Reproducibility question: the original restart probe (whose receipt is the most cited witness of the empty-configuration case, including its own non-replay and snapshot controls in one execution) is repeated once from its retained inputs in a clean copy, to confirm that the primary witness and both in-harness controls reproduce together. Reproducibility question: the partial-restart experiment is repeated once from its retained inputs in a clean copy, because that harness contains the timing-dependent half of the progress claim (which node leads after two of three voters restart) as well as the structural half (a live quorum that cannot elect once the configured voter stops). Correction of the repeat target: the repeat just executed (receipt 8f0b76d0cd49441c81ecb603f1fcd527) ran the superseded revision of the partial-restart experiment (experiment a8b8d696ac934beda1434a93b5d7758f-experiment), whose captured harness still used helpers declared in a sibling file and therefore failed to build before any test ran. The corrected, self-contained revision of that same harness is experiment b826595f01b844f9b95efe7b29d757dd-experiment (retained receipt 7afe8c0403874dbeb0a917a3ee9ed837); the repeat is re-requested against that revision. Reproducibility question: the revision carrying the client-contract observation is repeated once from its retained inputs, because that observation requires the stale leader to still consider itself leader when the confirmation is issued and when the old majority elects, which is schedule-sensitive (one earlier revision saw the leader step down first). Reproducibility question: the revision carrying the trigger boundary is repeated once from its retained inputs, to confirm that the shallow case keeps the committed membership (the condition that pins the trigger to a configuration entry inside the replayed prefix) while the same execution reproduces the resurrection and the accepted write in the failing case. Reproducibility question: the latent-trap experiment is repeated once from its retained inputs, because its contrast (a good outcome while nothing is staged, a lost configuration once the flag-on path has staged a commit index) is what pins the trigger to the persisted commit index, and it is the newest harness in the set with a single execution so far. The persisted commit index that the trigger names is written by the running node itself: tryStageCommitIndex (raft.go 1392-1404) stages the commit index into the store only when RestoreCommittedLogs is on and the store implements CommitTrackingLogStore, which is why the causal-refinement receipts can stage zero with the flag first enabled and nine after the node has run with it.

investigations.question: Does a node restarted with RestoreCommittedLogs=true, whose newest configuration entry is inside the persisted commit index and has no covering snapshot, still know that configuration after NewRaft returns?
investigations.hypothesis: No. restoreFromCommittedLogs sets lastApplied to the persisted commit index, so the configuration scan starts after the committed prefix and never calls processConfigurationLogEntry for the configuration entry that only exists in the log. r.configurations.latest stays empty (or stays at the snapshot configuration), so the node loses its own membership context, cannot start elections, and skips the membership checks when granting votes.
investigations.discriminator: Restart the same durable state twice: with RestoreCommittedLogs=true and with RestoreCommittedLogs=false. Predict servers_after=0 and no re-election with the feature on, versus servers_after=1 and a successful re-election with it off. A third run takes a snapshot before restart to show that a snapshot-carried configuration masks the loss (servers_after=1), separating the scanning bound from generic restart damage.

investigations.question: When RestoreCommittedLogs makes a restarted leader forget a committed removal, does the resurrected voter let that leader commit and report success for entries that the configuration committed in the log requires another member (B) to accept?
investigations.hypothesis: Yes: A's in-memory configuration still contains the removed voter C, so A's commitment quorum is computed over {A,B,C} and an entry acknowledged by A and C counts as committed even though the configuration committed in the log is {A,B}; A applies it and the client is told it succeeded although B, a member required for any quorum of the committed configuration, never received the entry.
investigations.discriminator: Same cluster and stores with the flag on and off: shut down C, remove it, commit further entries, restart the leader, bring C back so it catches up, partition B, then apply one entry on the leader. Prediction with the flag: the Apply returns success, the leader's commit and applied indexes advance to the new entry, and the entry is absent from B (and from every quorum of {A,B}). Prediction without the flag: the leader's configuration is {A,B}, so the same partition makes the same Apply fail.

investigations.question: When RestoreCommittedLogs makes a restarted leader forget a voter whose addition is committed in its own log, does the resulting smaller in-memory quorum let it accept and apply entries that only a minority of the committed voters hold?
investigations.hypothesis: Yes: with the added voter D absent from the restarted leader's configuration, its quorum is two of {A,B,C} instead of three of {A,B,C,D}, so a partition that leaves only A and B connected still lets it commit and apply an entry, and the client is told the write succeeded although a quorum of the committed configuration never received it.
investigations.discriminator: Four voters {A,B,C}+D added after a snapshot, further commits, then restart the leader with the flag on and off; partition C and D from A and apply one entry. Prediction with the flag: the Apply succeeds and only A and B hold the entry; prediction without the flag: the same partition makes the Apply fail.

investigations.question: When a node's in-memory configuration is empty after a restart with RestoreCommittedLogs, what can an operator actually do: does live bootstrap on the running node repair it, and does the documented RecoverCluster path on the stopped node repair it?
investigations.hypothesis: Live bootstrap does not help, because it refuses when the cluster is not new (existing term, log and snapshots), while RecoverCluster does repair the node: it reads the existing state, writes a snapshot carrying the supplied configuration and truncates the log, so the next NewRaft restores that configuration from the snapshot instead of from the skipped log prefix.
investigations.discriminator: Single-voter cluster bootstrapped, commands committed, node restarted with the flag so its configuration is empty; then (a) call BootstrapCluster on the running node and record the error and the configuration size, and (b) stop the node, run RecoverCluster with the same stores and the original configuration, start it again and record the configuration size and whether it leads.

gaps.question: Can the silently-created two-server change ({A,B,C} -> {A,B,E}, committed with A plus a promoted caught-up nonvoter E while B is partitioned) let the old majority {B,C} elect a leader in a higher term that then truncates A's committed entry X when the partition heals, and can the two sides therefore hold leaders of different terms over the same log?

interpretations.rationale: Summary of the current account for this question: the trigger is RestoreCommittedLogs=true with a CommitTrackingLogStore, a log whose newest configuration entry is at or below the persisted commit index, and no snapshot whose ConfigurationIndex covers that entry. Under that trigger the restarted node reconstructs its configuration only from the snapshot, so three consequence classes follow, each with retained control-backed receipts, plus a client-contract consequence recorded further below: (a) a missing membership context - empty configuration when there is no snapshot, which stops all campaigns and leaves a live quorum unable to elect (receipts 430d7ba602ed4666bdfe63a96c71e2fc, 4f4a771f03b649c2a5703b0ff279ff3a, 7afe8c0403874dbeb0a917a3ee9ed837); (b) decisions taken from a stale base - a single AddVoter becomes the two-server change {A,B,C}->{A,B,E}, which silently drops a voter, and with a partitioned old voter produces concurrent leaders over the same log, truncation of the entry the stale leader had committed and divergent FSM state (receipts d2d1cb0951b74a2984ec525710e4c740, 6f9feceeefb245c288a7fd1f4497b83c, 11dea1fdcb6d4f089a373fe6c1d3a36e and e5ad9e5149fa4255b61e7826bf6b8064); (c) stale membership accounting - a resurrected removed voter or a forgotten added voter makes the leader accept writes that the configuration committed in the log has not acknowledged (receipts 226f9762f0b444f69c154b35fe0788f3 with 7adf927d528b4a74942c03b155aa8557, and b1daa1f4c9444b8d857bc7e0ab761691 with ec2c61af79bd42d7a5fe00657b7aeb22). Boundary: a snapshot covering the newest configuration entry, or leaving the flag at its default, removes every one of these observations in the controls, and once the stale configuration is adopted nothing re-reads the log for configurations, so it persists until one of three events repairs it: a snapshot is installed (the configuration comes from the snapshot metadata), a later configuration entry reaches the node through appendEntries and is processed by processConfigurationLogEntry (raft.go 1569-1578, which installs the full membership the leader computed), or the node is restarted without the flag. In the empty-configuration cases the first two repairs need a leader, which is exactly what the empty configuration prevents. A repeat of the simultaneous-restart experiment reproduced the same failure and control values, so the headline progress claim also rests on two scored executions. Three independent receipts, all retained. (1) 430d7ba602ed4666bdfe63a96c71e2fc index 1: with RestoreCommittedLogs=true and no snapshot the restarting node returns with an empty configuration (servers_after=0 against servers_before=1), never campaigns again in a 3s opportunity, and logs 'no known peers, aborting election'; both the non-replay run (index 3) and the snapshot run (index 5) keep the configuration and re-elect. (2) d2d1cb0951b74a2984ec525710e4c740 index 1: with a snapshot carrying {A,B}@1 and a committed AddVoter C at index 8 with staged commit 11, the restarted node reports 2 servers while its continuously running peer reports 3 and its own log still holds the newest configuration entry; index 3: a later AddVoter E then returns no error and both nodes converge on 3 members without C (contains_c_final=false), i.e. a legitimately added voter is silently removed from the cluster by a change computed from the stale base. (3) edfd3c204c654542a8bdb4263f290d4d index 1: the isolated control with RestoreCommittedLogs=false scores holds (servers_after=1 against the same bootstrapped voter), so the replayed committed prefix, not restart itself, is the cause. (4) 4f4a771f03b649c2a5703b0ff279ff3a index 1: restarting all three voters at once with the flag leaves servers_after=[0,0,0] and nodes_with_full_config=0 with no leader in a six-second opportunity, while the same procedure without the flag scores holds at index 3 (nodes_with_full_config=3, leader elected) - a cluster-wide progress loss, not a single node's lost context. (5) 7afe8c0403874dbeb0a917a3ee9ed837: with only two of three voters restarted, the untouched configured voter leads with the configuration-less nodes' votes (index 0, servers_after=[0,0,3]); once that voter stops, the two remaining live, fully up-to-date voters cannot elect a leader in six seconds at 50ms timeouts (index 1, log last index 13 on both), while the control without the flag re-elects immediately (index 3). Source chain: restoreFromCommittedLogs raises lastApplied to the persisted commit index (api.go 723-755); the configuration scan then begins at max(lastSnapshot,lastApplied)+1 (api.go 611-613), so configuration entries inside the committed prefix are never fed to their only producer processConfigurationLogEntry (raft.go 1605-1623) unless a snapshot carries them (api.go 645-689). With Servers empty the follower refuses to campaign (raft.go 230-234 on every heartbeat timeout, raft.go 214-251) and both vote handlers skip their membership checks (raft.go 1663-1672, 1780-1784); with Servers stale, appendConfigurationEntry derives the next membership from that stale base (raft.go 1204-1241, configuration.go 224-302) once the admission gate sees latest==committed (raft.go 654-664). (6) 79d93a5aaad448888cc04214be8f2ad8: with A's configuration coming from a snapshot ({A,B}) while its log holds the newer {A,B,C} entry, AddVoter E returned no error and the silently created two-server change committed at index 11 with A's commit index at 11 and E holding the same LogConfiguration entry (parsed index 2), while B stayed at log index 10 with the old membership; the old majority {B,C} then elected B in term 4 while A was still leader in term 3 (parsed index 3, a_still_leader=true), and after the partition healed A's entry 11 was a LogNoop of term 4 rather than the committed configuration entry (parsed index 4, committed_entry_truncated=true). Receipt 6f9feceeefb245c288a7fd1f4497b83c from the corrected harness scored both comparisons: entry at index 11 truncated after heal (violated, witness index 4) and a_still_leader=true while the old side elected B in term 4 (violated, witness index 3), with the silent change itself at index 2 (change_err nil, committed=true, LogConfiguration on A and E, B at log index 10). The repeat receipt 11dea1fdcb6d4f089a373fe6c1d3a36e reproduced the same outcome under schedule variation (setup catch-up indices differed: C ended at log index 8 instead of 9): silent change committed at index 11 with entry type LogConfiguration on A and E (index 2), B elected in term 4 while A still led in term 3 (index 3, comparison violated), and the entry truncated after healing (index 4, comparison violated). Receipt e5ad9e5149fa4255b61e7826bf6b8064 (extended harness) scores both comparisons violated with witness index 5: the entry at the created index is truncated after healing, and after a client command returned success and was acknowledged and committed on the {A,B,E} leader (parsed index 3: write_applied=true, applied_a=12, fsm_a_logs=6) the FSM contents differ afterwards (fsm_a_logs=6 versus fsm_b_logs=5), so the client-visible effect survives only on the node whose log lost the entry.  A fourth consequence direction belongs to the client contracts: on the same stale leader, VerifyLeader confirms leadership from the stale quorum while a different majority of the committed configuration elects a leader in a higher term (receipt 1f95cb0a02bc4577a5a9f1ab627fe903, witness index 6), so the read-safety protection clients rely on is not effective in that state. Why the competing-majority outcome is attributable to the stale base rather than to the partition: with a correct configuration the same partition geometry cannot commit the change at all, because the change installs its own membership into the commitment and that membership still contains the partitioned voter, so its quorum cannot be reached (a single-server change from {A,B,C} needs two of three including the partitioned member's replacement geometry, and in the four-voter case the new quorum is three of four). The stale base both shrinks the base the change is computed from and replaces a voter, which is why the new member set's quorum can be met by A plus one other node while the partitioned voter stays out - and that is precisely what the D2 receipts show, with the control mode refusing the same write under the committed membership. Mechanism locators for the two steps that turn the stale base into those outcomes: the new configuration is installed into the leader's commitment as soon as the change entry is appended (raft.go 1236-1241), which is what lets the silently created member set be acknowledged by the stale leader plus one other node, and appendEntries clears a conflicting log suffix when terms differ (raft.go 1522-1553), which is what removes the entry the stale leader had committed once the higher-term leader reaches it; the vote freshness checks that keep the removed voter itself from winning are at raft.go 1731-1746 and 1812-1828.

9c549c026d7341f2b1e328826eac6dc3-gap-0.explanation: Resolved by retained receipt d2d1cb0951b74a2984ec525710e4c740: the restarted node adopts the snapshot-carried configuration when the newest configuration entry lies inside the replayed committed prefix (comparison 0 violated, witness index 1: servers_after=2 while the peer reports 3 and the newest configuration entry index 8 is below the staged commit index 11), and that stale base changes a real decision (comparison 2 violated, witness index 3: AddVoter E returned no error and both nodes ended with 3 members and contains_c_final=false, so voter C was silently removed). The same receipt's control mode kept 3 members and ended with 4 including C (observed at parsed index 5; that comparison was scored unknown because both modes shared a result event name, which the dedicated control experiment has now replaced with a scored holds).

a8b8d696ac934beda1434a93b5d7758f-gap-1.explanation: Resolved affirmatively by retained receipts 6f9feceeefb245c288a7fd1f4497b83c, 11dea1fdcb6d4f089a373fe6c1d3a36e, 1f95cb0a02bc4577a5a9f1ab627fe903 and 108a83830e904d90a9236738033c2c74: the silently created two-server change {A,B,C} -> {A,B,E} commits on the stale leader A plus the promoted, caught-up nonvoter E while the old voter B is partitioned (witness index 2 in each execution: change_err nil, committed true, the configuration entry present on A and on E, B still one index short); the old majority {B,C} then elects B in a higher term while A still leads its own configuration with E's acknowledgements (witness index 3 or 6: old_leader B in term 4 with a_still_leader true); and after the partition heals A's committed entry is replaced by the new leader's entry (witness index 7, committed_entry_truncated true), leaving the two sides with different logs and different applied state (fsm_a_logs 6 against fsm_b_logs 5). The direct route the earlier answer identified as impossible stays impossible - a voter that never receives the entry is strictly behind and is refused by voters that hold it (raft.go 1731-1746, 1812-1828) - which is exactly why the construction needs the entry to commit without one old voter, made possible by the promoted nonvoter and by the new configuration entering the commitment on append (raft.go 1236-1241).

1ed9540f22fe4fa9bef3b3bda88e22e8-gap-2.explanation: Resolved by retained receipt 6f9feceeefb245c288a7fd1f4497b83c (scored): the silent two-server change {A,B,C} -> {A,B,E} committed on A plus the promoted caught-up nonvoter E (parsed index 2: change_err nil, x_index 11, committed=true, entry type LogConfiguration on A and on E, A commit index 11, B still at log index 10); the old majority {B,C} elected B in term 4 while A was still leader in term 3 (parsed index 3, comparison violated with witness 3), i.e. two concurrent leaders with disjoint support over the same log; and after healing, A's entry at index 11 became a LogNoop of term 4 (parsed index 4, comparison violated with witness 4), so the entry committed under the configuration recorded in the logs was truncated on the node that had committed it. The earlier receipt 79d93a5aaad448888cc04214be8f2ad8 reproduced the same observations but its comparisons were unscored because of my identity wiring; it is retained as the superseded revision of the same harness.

knowledge.assertion: Used for the claim that a configuration entry inside the replayed committed prefix is not restored, which is why the restarted node ends up with the snapshot configuration (empty when there is no snapshot).

Used for the mechanism by which the stale membership drives configuration-change admission, the next-membership derivation, the commitment installed on append, the election quorum, the lease check and leadership confirmation, and hence for the silent voter drop, the premature commits and the concurrent-leader outcome.
Used for the repair-path statements: which paths restore a configuration held only in the log, and that live bootstrap and an incoming snapshot for a complete-log node do not.

counterevidence: The isolated control receipt edfd3c204c654542a8bdb4263f290d4d scores holds with the identical restart and no snapshot (servers_after=1), so the loss is caused by replaying the committed prefix, not by restart, snapshot absence, or the commit-tracking store.

The snapshot run inside the first receipt (index 5) keeps the configuration, so the defect requires the newest configuration entry to be inside the skipped prefix; a snapshot taken after the change masks it.
Voter C never runs in the two-voter probe, so nothing in the receipts shows C resisting or noticing its removal; the claim is about the configuration the running nodes decide with.

The cluster-wide receipt 4f4a771f03b649c2a5703b0ff279ff3a scores the control comparison holds (index 3, nodes_with_full_config=3) and the failing case violated (index 1, nodes_with_full_config=0), so the empty configuration after a simultaneous restart is specific to the replayed committed prefix.

Receipt 7afe8c0403874dbeb0a917a3ee9ed837 scores the control comparison holds (index 3: the two live voters re-elect a leader without the flag) and the failing case violated (index 1: after the configured voter stops, no leader among the two live voters although both hold every committed entry, log last index 13 on both), so the loss of electability is tied to the missing configuration rather than to the restart or the shutdown.

The dual-majority path needs a caught-up nonvoter E so the silent change can commit without the partitioned voter B; without such a node the change would need B's acknowledgement and B would then hold the new membership.

Two independent executions of the corrected dual-majority experiment (receipts 6f9feceeefb245c288a7fd1f4497b83c and 11dea1fdcb6d4f089a373fe6c1d3a36e) produced the same entry index, the same concurrent leadership and the same truncation, so the outcome is reproducible rather than a single-run timing artifact.

In that extended execution the stale leader had already stepped down when the old side's leader was sampled (index 4, a_still_leader=false), which is why leader concurrency is reported as an observed window from the two earlier executions rather than as a comparison in the current harness.

Repeat receipt c1dcda29549b48c7a775adfc2e9a4bda reproduced the simultaneous-restart outcome exactly (servers_after [0,0,0], nodes_with_full_config 0, no leader in the observation window; control [3,3,3] with a leader elected at index 3), so the cluster-wide progress loss is reproducible under schedule variation (the staged commit indices differed from the first run: [11 10 11] against [11 11 9]).

Repeat receipt e0ef28c2bc89481aa6b3af478422de7c reproduced all three modes of the original probe with the same values: with RestoreCommittedLogs and no snapshot the node returns with an empty configuration and does not lead again (index 1), while the non-replay mode keeps its configuration and leads (index 3) and the snapshot mode keeps its configuration and leads (index 5).

Repeat receipt 2963a0b01d97404dbf946e7b87a214f8 reproduced the partial-restart outcome exactly (two restarted voters with empty configurations, the untouched voter leading at index 2 with nodes_with_full=1, then no leader among the two live voters holding log index 13 apiece; control re-electing at index 0), so the live-quorum progress loss is reproducible as well.

The revised dual-majority execution (receipt 1f95cb0a02bc4577a5a9f1ab627fe903) scored all three comparisons as predicted: the committed entry is truncated after healing (violated, witness 7), the FSMs diverge after an acknowledged write (violated, witness 7, fsm_a_logs 6 against fsm_b_logs 5), and the stale leader confirmed leadership while the old majority led in a higher term (violated, witness 6: verify_ok true, old_leader B in term 4, a_still_leader true).

The repeat of the client-contract revision (receipt 108a83830e904d90a9236738033c2c74) reproduced all three comparison outcomes (truncation violated at witness 7, FSM divergence violated at witness 7, confirmation-while-another-leader violated at witness 6 with verify_ok true, old_leader B in term 4 and A still leading), so that consequence is reproducible.

The repair execution also acts as counterevidence against reading the stale configuration as irrecoverable: a later configuration entry from a correctly configured leader restored the forgotten voter on the restarted node (receipt 6d6abaf163524e64878c6c9810de2461, comparison and witness index 5).

Boundary control: with the same operations but without the commits that push the persisted commit index past the removal entry, the restarted node keeps the committed membership and the removed voter stays removed (receipt 457abd18451d4fd18ed506ae7f5c5391, comparison and witness index 9), so the loss is tied to the entry lying inside the replayed prefix and not to the restart or the removal itself.

The boundary control repeated: receipt 4fe974e4e3cc491984791b8a812c5886 reproduced every comparison of the boundary revision (resurrection violated at index 1, premature commit violated at index 3, flag-off control holding at index 7, and the shallow case holding at index 9 with two servers and the removed voter absent), so the trigger boundary is reproducible and not a schedule artifact.

Counterevidence that limits the impact of the cluster-wide loss rather than the finding: the same stores, restarted once more with the flag disabled, came back fully configured and elected a leader (receipt 81163da076c64417bd48e0f79260d73d, comparison and witness index 2), so the state is operator-recoverable without touching durable data.

Causal refinement, observed rather than argued: the same stores and the same flag produced a good outcome while nothing had been staged and the failure once the flag-on path had staged a commit index (receipt 656e33fb90f24c58a94928eeeeb938aa, comparison holds at index 1 and violated at index 3), so the deciding condition is the persisted commit index named in the trigger, not merely enabling the feature.

Causal refinement reproduced: repeat receipt 202311f4911e4af5828d49134f37811c produced the identical values and outcomes (staged zero with the configuration kept through the first flagged restart, holds at index 1; staged nine afterwards and the configuration lost on the next one, violated at witness index 3), so the contrast that pins the trigger to the persisted commit index is stable across executions.

Record-keeping limitation, not a counterexample to any claim: the stored repair Fact lists four sources and three receipts while its corrected statement and conditions were merged; the missing receipt (6d6abaf163524e64878c6c9810de2461 index 5) and the four named source anchors are cited here and in the interpretations that rely on them, so no claim rests on the shortened list.
limitations: All executions are in-process in-memory clusters at protocol version 3 with 50ms heartbeat/election timeouts and a single committed configuration change; joint-consensus or multi-step changes are not exercised.
The finding is specific to RestoreCommittedLogs=true with a CommitTrackingLogStore; with the flag disabled the same durable state recovers normally in every receipt.

The configuration-less nodes still act as voters in other respects (they granted the configured voter's election win in receipt 7afe8c0403874dbeb0a917a3ee9ed837, index 0), which is why the cluster survived until that voter stopped; this is read from the receipt and from the membership checks being skipped for an empty configuration (raft.go 1663-1672, 1780-1784).

In that probe the partitioned side elects its leader with 3s election timeouts (reloaded to keep the restarted leader from losing the first election), so the interval is seconds; the ordering it demonstrates does not depend on those particular values.

The dual-majority probe has no control variant: with the flag disabled the leader's configuration is current, so the same AddVoter is a single-server change and cannot create disjoint majorities (nextConfiguration over the current configuration, configuration.go 224-302).

Leader concurrency on the two sides was observed with A still leading in four executions (receipts 6f9feceeefb245c288a7fd1f4497b83c, 11dea1fdcb6d4f089a373fe6c1d3a36e, 1f95cb0a02bc4577a5a9f1ab627fe903 and 108a83830e904d90a9236738033c2c74) while one revision of the harness observed A already stepped down when the old side's leader was sampled, so the window is real but its length is schedule-dependent; the reproducible consequences are the truncation of the committed entry and the resulting FSM divergence.

The child question is now established by retained receipt 226f9762f0b444f69c154b35fe0788f3 (resurrected membership and a write applied on the leader with B, required by the committed configuration, never receiving the entry; control refuses the same write), so the parents' consequence list includes premature commitment under a stale membership.

Two consequences reached by later receipts are no longer pending: the cluster-wide and partial-restart progress losses (receipts 4f4a771f03b649c2a5703b0ff279ff3a and 7afe8c0403874dbeb0a917a3ee9ed837) and the premature-commit-under-a-stale-membership consequence (receipt 226f9762f0b444f69c154b35fe0788f3 with its repeat 7adf927d528b4a74942c03b155aa8557).

A source check of which snapshot the library considers newest found the expected protection: SnapshotStore implementations rank candidates by term then index (file_snapshot.go 535-547 with List at 286), so the newest snapshot is selected; no evidence of a snapshot-selection defect was found, and none is claimed.

The third consequence direction is now established by retained receipt b1daa1f4c9444b8d857bc7e0ab761691: a restarted leader that forgets an added voter accepted a write held by only two of the four committed voters, while the control refused it.

A check of the captured documentation found no statement about this feature outside the source: RestoreCommittedLogs and CommitTrackingLogStore appear only in config.go, log.go and api.go, and never in README.md, docs/README.md, docs/apply.md, docs/divergence.md, membership.md or CHANGELOG.md (those files do mention snapshots elsewhere, so the search itself is sound). The only normative text is the Config field comment, which requires the commit-tracking store but nothing about snapshots or configuration recovery, so no documented caller duty defeats the premise.

In the original probe and its repeat the two control modes share the comparison event names with the failing mode, so their comparisons are scored unknown; the scored control for the non-replay restart comes from the separate isolated-control experiment (receipt edfd3c204c654542a8bdb4263f290d4d, holds).

Correction of the repair-path statement: an earlier version of the summary said only a snapshot install or an operator restart repairs a stale configuration. A later configuration entry does too, because appendEntries processes new configuration entries and installs the membership encoded in them (raft.go 1569-1578); the three repair paths are now stated explicitly. The client-contract consequence is now established by retained receipt 1f95cb0a02bc4577a5a9f1ab627fe903: VerifyLeader returned success on the stale-membership leader (its own acknowledgement plus the promoted voter's) in the same execution in which the old majority elected B in term 4 while that leader still considered itself leader, so the documented protection against returning stale data does not hold in this state.

Boundary that follows: repair needs a correctly configured leader, so it is available where the stale nodes are a minority (the forgotten-voter case) and unavailable where the empty configuration prevents any leader from being elected (the cluster-wide and partial-restart cases).

Boundary of the empty-configuration case, kept explicit because it limits the consequence: what is lost is membership context and the ability to campaign, not data flow. In the partial-restart receipts (7afe8c0403874dbeb0a917a3ee9ed837 and its repeat 2963a0b01d97404dbf946e7b87a214f8) the two configuration-less nodes still appended and applied entries up to log index 13 while the correctly configured voter led, and they still granted the votes that let it win, so replication through a configured leader continues; the observable harm is their empty self-view (no campaigns, no peers) and, once the configured voter stops, the cluster-wide loss of electability recorded in those same receipts.

Reachability boundary on the snapshot repair path: although an installed snapshot does carry the configuration (raft.go 1953-1961), a leader sends a snapshot only when the follower lacks entries the leader has already compacted, and a node whose configuration was lost this way has a complete log (the loss comes from skipping entries, not from missing them), so no snapshot is sent to it in these scenarios (with the caveat, found while re-reading the snapshot path, that a leader-side user restore leaves a hole above such a node's next index and does send it one, replication.go 222-224 with raft.go 1097-1199). The snapshot path therefore repairs new or behind nodes, while a stale-but-complete node is repaired only by an operator restart without the flag or by a later configuration entry from a correctly configured leader, as executed.

Operator recovery is now executed (receipt 0440f054115e44f4a0234c7a4ef67150): in the empty-configuration state live bootstrap refuses with 'bootstrap only works on new clusters' and leaves the node empty (violated, index 1), while RecoverCluster on the stopped node restores the supplied configuration and the node leads again within three seconds (holds, index 2). The repair picture is therefore complete and operational: a later configuration entry from a correctly configured leader, a restart with the flag disabled, or RecoverCluster on a stopped node; not live bootstrap, and not an incoming snapshot for a node whose log is already complete.

The operator remediation for the cluster-wide case is now executed (receipt 81163da076c64417bd48e0f79260d73d): the flagged simultaneous restart left every voter empty with no leader (violated, index 1, staged commit indices [11 11 11]), and stopping the same three nodes and restarting them on the same stores with the flag disabled restored the configuration on all three and produced a leader (holds at index 2, nodes_with_full_config 3, leader index 1; control unchanged at index 4). The consequence of the headline progress loss is therefore bounded: it is in-memory and reversible by an ordinary restart, with no durable state discarded and no configuration change needed, but nothing in-protocol can repair it while it lasts.

Precision on what the truncation removes, taken from the same receipts rather than reasoned: in both executions that carry the client write (e5ad9e5149fa4255b61e7826bf6b8064 index 5 and 1f95cb0a02bc4577a5a9f1ab627fe903 index 7) the stale leader's log end falls from index 12 to 11 after healing while its applied index stays at 12 and its FSM still holds six commands against the new leader's five. The entry removed is therefore not only the configuration change at index 11 but also the client command the leader had committed and applied at index 12, and the two sides' applied state differs by exactly that command. This is the client-visible form of the safety violation: an acknowledged write is deleted from the log of the node that acknowledged it, while the divergent FSM keeps its effect.

The causal refinement is executed (receipt 656e33fb90f24c58a94928eeeeb938aa): the cluster that had only run with the flag disabled carried a staged commit index of 0 and kept its configuration through the first flagged restart (comparison holds, index 1), then staged 9 through its own writes while the flag was on (index 2) and lost the configuration on the next flagged restart (violated, witness index 3, zero servers and no leader). The trigger is therefore the persisted commit index relative to the newest configuration entry, not the flag by itself, and the first restart after enabling the feature can look harmless.

The latent-trap experiment has been executed twice with identical values (receipts 656e33fb90f24c58a94928eeeeb938aa and 202311f4911e4af5828d49134f37811c), so the causal refinement rests on a reproduced contrast rather than a single run.

Detection, from the fields this investigation already read rather than from a new API: GetConfiguration and Stats report the node's in-memory configuration and its index (api.go 1231-1237 and the GetConfiguration accessor), so the state is found by comparing that configuration with the configuration a peer reports or with the newest configuration entry in the node's own store, not by a threshold on indexes. The two forms observed here are an empty in-memory configuration (the empty case, seen as zero servers and zero peers while the node still holds a complete log) and an in-memory configuration older than the newest configuration entry in that node's log (the stale case, e.g. two servers while peers report three or four). One caution against a false positive: latest_configuration_index being below commit_index is normal, because a configuration entry stays the latest until a later configuration entry appears while ordinary entries continue to commit, so that comparison alone does not indicate this state.

Protection direction, following directly from the traced mechanism rather than from any new claim: the state exists because the configuration scan begins after the replayed committed prefix (api.go 611-613), so scanning configuration entries from the snapshot index onward instead of from max(lastSnapshot, lastApplied)+1 would leave the replayed entries applied to the FSM while still rebuilding the configuration from the log; and because the failure is silent, a start-time check that compares the reconstructed configuration with the newest configuration entry the node's own log or snapshot carries (and refuses to serve, or reports, when a voter's configuration is empty or older than that entry) would surface the state where indexes alone cannot, since the log is complete and commit and applied indexes look healthy.

interpretations.rationale: Retained receipt b1daa1f4c9444b8d857bc7e0ab761691 scores all four comparisons as predicted. After a committed AddVoter D and a restart with RestoreCommittedLogs, the leader reports three servers and no longer contains D while the other three nodes report four (comparison 0 violated, witness index 1). With C and D disconnected, a single Apply on that leader succeeds: it commits and applies the entry at index 8 while C's log ends at 7 and D's at 6, so only two of the four committed voters hold it and the entry is not committed under the configuration in the log, which requires three (comparison 2 violated, witness index 3, voters_holding_entry=2, entry_on_committed_quorum=false). The controls hold: the same restart without the flag keeps four servers (index 5) and the same partition makes the write fail with 'leadership lost while committing log' (index 7). Mechanism: the in-memory configuration drives the quorum (configurationChangeChIfStable admits changes on stale indexes, appendConfigurationEntry derives membership from the stale base, commitment is installed from it on append), so a configuration missing a committed voter understates the quorum and lets the client be told a write succeeded.

knowledge.assertion: Used for why the understated membership lowers the quorum below the committed configuration's requirement, letting the leader accept an entry that only a minority of the committed voters holds.

counterevidence: The control mode on identical stores and the identical partition refuses the write, so the acceptance is attributable to the understated membership rather than to the partition.

Repeat receipt ec2c61af79bd42d7a5fe00657b7aeb22 scored the identical outcomes (membership violated at index 1, premature commit violated at index 3, controls hold at indices 5 and 7), so the observation is reproducible.

The revision carrying the repair phase scored all five comparisons as predicted (membership violated at index 1, premature commit violated at index 3, controls holding at indices 7 and 9, and the repair holding at index 5), so the understated-quorum consequence and the later repair of the same node are both reproducible in one execution.
limitations: The example uses four voters; the size of the understatement grows with the number of voters added after the snapshot, so this probe understates rather than overstates the margin.

The repeat execution reproduced the same values and outcomes (leader with three servers while the others have four, entry index 8 applied on A with C at 7 and D at 6, control refusing the write), so the understated-quorum observation is not a single-run artifact.

interpretations.rationale: Retained receipt 0440f054115e44f4a0234c7a4ef67150 answers what an operator can do in the state this investigation identified. The state itself reproduced (parsed index 0: zero servers, no leader within two seconds, staged commit 6, log last index 7). Live bootstrap on the running node failed with 'bootstrap only works on new clusters' and left the configuration empty (parsed index 1, comparison violated): that is the documented refusal, since BootstrapCluster checks HasExistingState and returns ErrCantBootstrap when a term, log or snapshot exists (api.go 260-267), which is exactly this state. RecoverCluster on the stopped node succeeded and the following NewRaft came up with one server and led within three seconds (parsed index 2, comparison holds): it restores any snapshot, replays the log into the supplied FSM, writes a new snapshot carrying the supplied configuration and truncates the log (api.go 321-448), so the next NewRaft takes its configuration from that snapshot instead of from the replayed prefix that the defect skips. The library therefore does provide a repair path for a stopped node, but not for a running one and not in-protocol; no defect is claimed about either behaviour, and the value of the observation is operational: it distinguishes a path that works from one that does not in the state the defect creates.

knowledge.assertion: Used to place the two observed operator paths within the recorded set of repair paths: RecoverCluster is one of them and live bootstrap is not.

counterevidence: The two outcomes point in opposite directions and both match the documented contracts, so neither is evidence against the finding: the repair that works requires stopping the node and supplying the configuration explicitly, while the running node cannot repair itself.
limitations: Single-voter cluster; RecoverCluster's success is shown on a node whose stores are otherwise intact, which is the state the defect leaves behind (complete log, missing in-memory configuration).
RecoverCluster is documented as an unsafe, explicit disaster-recovery operation; its success here is a repair capability, not a normal operating path.

result.summary: No change this turn and none warranted: update.json is retained exactly as applied, the controller confirms no_change with no execution requested, and the investigation has no open gaps or pending consequences — so I am stopping rather than churning the record. The account is complete and receipt-backed: a node restarted with RestoreCommittedLogs, whose newest configuration entry sits at or below the persisted commit index with no covering snapshot, comes back without that configuration (430d7ba602ed4666bdfe63a96c71e2fc, repeat e0ef28c2bc89481aa6b3af478422de7c, trigger pinned to the persisted commit index by 656e33fb90f24c58a94928eeeeb938aa and 202311f4911e4af5828d49134f37811c); the consequences are empty-configuration loss of electability cluster-wide and among a live quorum (4f4a771f03b649c2a5703b0ff279ff3a, 7afe8c0403874dbeb0a917a3ee9ed837 plus repeats), silent membership change with concurrent leaders, truncation of a committed client write and FSM divergence (6f9feceeefb245c288a7fd1f4497b83c, 1f95cb0a02bc4577a5a9f1ab627fe903, 108a83830e904d90a9236738033c2c74, e5ad9e5149fa4255b61e7826bf6b8064), premature commit under a resurrected removed voter and under a forgotten added voter (226f9762f0b444f69c154b35fe0788f3 and b1daa1f4c9444b8d857bc7e0ab761691 with repeats and the boundary 457abd18451d4fd18ed506ae7f5c5391), and VerifyLeader confirming a stale leader; the repairs are bounded to a later configuration entry (6d6abaf163524e64878c6c9810de2461), a flag-disabled restart (81163da076c64417bd48e0f79260d73d) and RecoverCluster on a stopped node (0440f054115e44f4a0234c7a4ef67150), with live bootstrap and an incoming snapshot to a complete-log node ruled out. One bookkeeping note carries forward for whoever reads the run next, unchanged from my earlier turns: the duplicate question node 4099b8f3cc5c45d2b3c3049ce5a5c0de-question-0 (same restart text, no interpretation) sits beside 9c549c026d7341f2b1e328826eac6dc3-question-0, which holds the interpretation 4099b8f3cc5c45d2b3c3049ce5a5c0de-interpretation-0; I left both untouched because repointing the interpretation would detach it from the history it belongs to, and the seconds left in this budget are not a safe window for that edit.
